title: From Text to Law: Usul al-Fiqh, the Schools and Ijtihad
bigQuestion: How did a book with only a few hundred legal verses become the root of whole libraries of law, and who decides what it requires today?

story.title: A Few Hundred Verses and a Library
story.kicker: A student counts the verses that give rules, then sees how many shelves grew from them.
paragraphs: Nadia's assignment was simple to state and hard to finish. Go through Pickthall's 1930 translation and mark every verse that gives a rule: do this, do not do that, this is allowed, this is forbidden. She started in Surah 2, Al-Baqarah, 'The Cow,' and the marks came fast. Fasting in 2:183. Debts and witnesses in 2:282. Divorce, inheritance, contracts. Then she reached the Mecca surahs near the back, and the marks almost stopped. Those chapters spoke of judgment, mercy and the signs of God in rain and mountains, not of contracts.

When she finished, her count sat near five hundred. Her teacher said scholars land in the same neighborhood, though they disagree about what counts as a legal verse. Out of more than six thousand verses, perhaps one in twelve gives a rule. Many of those rules are about worship: prayer, fasting, the pilgrimage. Fewer speak to crime, and only a handful name a fixed punishment.

That afternoon the class visited a university library in Chicago. The librarian led them past shelves that ran the length of a wall. Every volume was *fiqh*, Islamic jurisprudence: the reasoning of scholars about what God requires. Some sets were forty volumes long. Nadia asked how five hundred verses could become this. The librarian smiled and said, 'That is the whole story of Islamic law. The Qur'an gives the roots. Scholars grew the branches.'

Back at school, Nadia wrote her reflection. The Qur'an does not read like a law code, she said. It reads like a sermon that sometimes gives rules. So Muslim scholars had to build a method for turning a book of guidance into answers for cases the book never mentions: a new drug, a new kind of loan, a question about a heart transplant. That method has a name, *usul al-fiqh*, the roots of jurisprudence. This chapter is about how it works, who used it, and how it is debated now.
story.think: If a sacred text gives only a few hundred rules, what must its readers do when a question arises that the text never mentions? What choices does that leave them?

lessons.title: A Book That Is Not a Code
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an gives guidance and some rules, but it is not a law code, so Muslim scholars built a method to reason from it.
reading: Open the Qur'an anywhere and you will find praise of God, stories of earlier prophets, warnings about the last day and calls to be generous. Only here and there does the text stop and give a rule. Scholars who count the *legal verses* usually arrive somewhere between two hundred and five hundred, out of roughly 6,236 in the standard Kufan count. The exact number depends on what a reader decides to count. A verse that says 'be just' can be read as a rule or as a moral appeal.

The legal verses cluster in the surahs Muslims date to Medina, after 622, when the community had to run a town. Surah 2, Al-Baqarah, and Surah 4, An-Nisa, 'Women,' hold many of them: fasting, pilgrimage, marriage, divorce, inheritance, debts and the treatment of orphans. The Mecca surahs, which come from the earlier years, speak mostly of belief and conduct in general terms. Muslim scholars have long noticed this pattern and used it to date passages.

Because the Qur'an is not arranged as a code, Muslim scholars developed *fiqh*, jurisprudence, the human effort to work out what God requires in each case. They distinguish fiqh from *sharia*. Sharia, in the classical sense, is God's way as scholars understand it to exist; fiqh is the scholars' understanding, which can be wrong and can differ from one scholar to another. Many modern Muslim writers stress this distinction when the word sharia appears in the news, because a headline about 'sharia law' often means one fiqh opinion among many.

This chapter follows the method scholars built: what sources they used, how they ranked them, and why the same verse could yield different rulings in Baghdad, Cairo and Cordoba. It ends with how the method is debated now, including by Muslim jurists in the United States. Throughout, the aim is to describe, not to judge: what Muslims have said the law is, and how they have reasoned about it.

words.d: the verses of the Qur'an that state a rule; scholars count somewhere between 200 and 500, depending on how they count
Islamic jurisprudence; the human effort by scholars to work out what God requires in each case
God's way, as Muslim scholars understand it; distinct in classical usage from fiqh, the human understanding of it

lessons.title: Four Sources, In Order
lessons.mainIdea: Sunni usul al-fiqh names four sources of law in rank: the Qur'an, the Sunnah, consensus and analogy.
reading: The classical Sunni method, *usul al-fiqh* (the 'roots of jurisprudence'), names four sources and ranks them. First is the Qur'an. Second is the *Sunnah*, the practice and sayings of Muhammad, known through the hadith reports. Third is *ijma'*, consensus, the agreement of qualified scholars on a question. Fourth is *qiyas*, analogy, reasoning from a case the texts cover to a case they do not. A jurist works down the list: if the Qur'an is clear, stop; if not, look to the Sunnah; and so on.

The scholar most often credited with setting this order out is Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i, who died in 820 in Egypt. His book, the Risala, argued that the Sunnah explains the Qur'an and that the Qur'an itself commands obedience to the messenger. He cited 4:59, An-Nisa, which in Pickthall's 1930 translation calls believers to obey God, the messenger and those in authority. Historians note that jurists before al-Shafi'i used local custom and personal opinion more freely, and that his book helped tie law more tightly to reported hadith.

Analogy is the tool that makes the method stretch. The Qur'an in 5:90, Al-Ma'idah, forbids wine, which the text calls khamr. What about a drink made from dates, or a drug unknown in Arabia? The jurist asks why wine is forbidden. If the reason is that it clouds the mind, then anything that clouds the mind shares the ruling. That 'reason,' the illa, is the hinge of every analogy, and jurists argued for centuries about how to find it.

Consensus was the most disputed source. Whose agreement counts, and how could anyone know that every qualified scholar in every city agreed? Some limited it to the Prophet's companions; others accepted the agreement of the scholars of Medina. Shia jurists, as the next lessons show, ranked the sources differently and added the teaching of the Imams. Even within Sunni Islam, the four-source picture was an ideal that real jurists bent to fit their cases.

words.d: the 'roots of jurisprudence'; the method for deriving law from its sources
the practice and sayings of Muhammad, known through hadith; the second source of Sunni law
consensus; the agreement of qualified scholars on a legal question
analogy; reasoning from a case the texts cover to a case they do not, by finding the shared reason

lessons.title: Reading Commands and Prohibitions
lessons.mainIdea: Jurists sorted every act into five rulings and read the Qur'an's words closely to decide which one applied.
reading: Islamic law does not sort acts only into legal and illegal. Classical jurists used five categories, the *ahkam*: obligatory, recommended, permitted, disliked and forbidden. Prayer is obligatory. Extra fasting is recommended. Eating an apple is simply permitted. Wasting food is disliked. Theft is forbidden. Most of life falls into the wide middle, permitted, and jurists often quoted the principle that the default for ordinary things is permission unless a text forbids them.

To place an act, a jurist read the words of the text closely. Does a command in the Qur'an mean 'you must' or 'you may'? When 62:10, Al-Jumu'ah, tells believers to spread through the land and seek God's bounty after the Friday prayer, nearly all jurists read it as permission to go back to work, not a duty. When 2:183, Al-Baqarah, says that fasting is prescribed, they read a duty. Grammar, context and the way the Prophet's companions understood a verse all counted as evidence.

Jurists also asked whether a verse was general or specific, and whether a later verse changed an earlier one. The theory of *naskh*, abrogation, held that God could replace one ruling with another in the course of the revelation. Wine is the standard example: 2:219 says it has some benefit and great sin, 4:43 forbids prayer while drunk, and 5:90 tells believers to shun it. Most classical jurists read this as a sequence ending in prohibition. Modern scholars differ on how much abrogation there really is; some accept dozens of cases, some very few.

This close reading meant that two careful scholars could reach different rulings from the same verse. That was not seen as failure. A famous saying attributed to the Prophet in Sunni collections holds that a judge who reasons carefully and errs still earns a reward. Classical fiqh made room for disagreement, ikhtilaf, and whole books were written cataloging the differences between the schools.

words.d: the five rulings of Islamic law: obligatory, recommended, permitted, disliked and forbidden
abrogation; the theory that a later verse can replace the ruling of an earlier one
scholarly disagreement, accepted in classical fiqh as normal and even valuable

look.title: One Verb, Two Readings

The same grammatical form appears in 2:183, where fasting is 'prescribed.' Jurists read the first as permission (you may go back to work) and the second as obligation (you must fast).

Theft
Eating an apple

Analogy is forbidden in law
Only the Mecca surahs contain law

check.why: Naskh, abrogation, holds that a later verse can change an earlier ruling; the wine verses are the classic example.

check.q: How did classical fiqh treat disagreement between careful scholars?

As proof that one scholar was a heretic

As a matter for the caliph alone to settle
check.why: Ikhtilaf, scholarly disagreement, was accepted; jurists wrote whole works comparing the schools' differences.

lessons.title: Four Sunni Schools
lessons.mainIdea: By about 900, Sunni law had settled into four schools, each named for an early scholar, that differ in method more than in belief.
reading: Sunni Muslims follow one of four *madhhabs*, schools of law, each named for a scholar of the eighth or ninth century. The Hanafi school looks to Abu Hanifa, who died in 767 in Baghdad and favored careful reasoning and analogy. The Maliki school looks to Malik ibn Anas, who died in 795 in Medina and gave weight to the practice of that city. The Shafi'i school follows al-Shafi'i, who died in 820. The Hanbali school follows Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who died in 855 and preferred hadith over reasoned opinion wherever a report could be found.

Historians stress that none of these men set out to found a school. Their students collected their opinions, and over the next two centuries those collections became organized traditions with their own teachers, books and colleges. By about the year 1000, most Sunni scholars belonged to one of them. Other early schools, such as that of al-Awza'i in Syria, faded away. The four survived, historians suggest, partly because rulers and endowed colleges supported them.

The schools mostly agree on belief and on the pillars of practice. Their differences lie in method and detail: how to weigh a weak hadith, when to use analogy, whether local custom counts, how to hold the hands in prayer. Geography spread them: Hanafis across Turkey, Central Asia and South Asia; Malikis across North and West Africa; Shafi'is in Egypt, East Africa and Southeast Asia; Hanbalis in the Arabian Peninsula. Estimates vary, but the Hanafi school is usually described as the largest.

Sunni scholars have long taught that all four are valid. The Amman Message of 2004, which a later chapter discusses, restated this by listing the schools whose followers count as Muslims. In an American mosque, a Hanafi from Pakistan may pray beside a Maliki from Senegal and a Shafi'i from Indonesia, each following a slightly different form. Muslim writers often point to this as the tradition's built-in room for difference.

words.d: a school of Islamic law; Sunnis recognize four, named for Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ibn Hanbal
the school named for Abu Hanifa (d. 767), known for reasoned analogy; usually described as the largest
the school named for Ahmad ibn Hanbal (d. 855), which prefers hadith over reasoned opinion

lessons.title: The Ja'fari School and Shia Law
lessons.mainIdea: Shia law follows the Ja'fari school, which adds the teaching of the Imams to the sources and gives reason a larger place than analogy.
reading: Most Shia Muslims follow the *Ja'fari* school, named for Ja'far al-Sadiq, the sixth Imam, who died in 765 in Medina. Sunni sources also honor him as a teacher; tradition says that Abu Hanifa and Malik both studied with him. For Shia Muslims, however, the Imams are not only teachers. They are the divinely guided successors of the Prophet, and their sayings carry the authority of the Sunnah. Shia hadith collections therefore include reports from the Imams as well as from Muhammad.

The sources of Ja'fari law are the Qur'an, the Sunnah (of the Prophet and the Imams), consensus and *aql*, reason. Most Shia jurists rejected Sunni-style analogy, arguing that guessing at God's reasons is unsafe; they preferred to reason from clear principles. Consensus, in their view, is valid because it reveals the view of the Imam. Shia Muslims believe the twelfth Imam went into hiding in the ninth century and will return, so scholars stand in for him in the meantime.

In practice this made the trained jurist, the mujtahid, central to Shia religious life. Since the eighteenth century, a school of thought called Usuli has held that every believer who is not a jurist must follow a living jurist's rulings. The most senior are called marja', 'source of imitation,' and today several live in Najaf, Iraq, and Qom, Iran. A smaller school, the Akhbari, preferred to rely on the reports of the Imams alone and gave jurists less room.

On most everyday questions, Ja'fari rulings resemble Sunni ones, with some well-known differences in inheritance, temporary marriage and the details of prayer. Sunni and Shia jurists have often criticized one another, and at times persecuted one another, yet the Amman Message of 2004 listed the Ja'fari school among the recognized schools. Describing these differences, and their shared roots, is part of studying the Qur'an's law fairly.

words.d: the main Shia school of law, named for Ja'far al-Sadiq, the sixth Imam (d. 765)
in Shia Islam, one of the divinely guided successors of the Prophet whose teaching carries legal authority
reason; a source of law in the Ja'fari school, preferred over Sunni-style analogy
a senior Shia jurist whose rulings ordinary believers follow; several live in Najaf and Qom

look.title: Two Ways Past a Silent Text
look.text: A Sunni jurist facing a question the texts do not answer reaches for qiyas: find the reason behind a known ruling and extend it. A Ja'fari jurist tends to reach for aql, reason from clear principles, and for the sayings of the Imams, saying that guessing at God's reasons is unsafe. Both agree that the Qur'an and the Prophet's Sunnah come first.
look.prompt: What is the difference between extending a rule by analogy and reasoning from a principle? Can you think of a case where the two methods might give different answers?

check.why: Shia Muslims hold the Imams to be divinely guided, so their reports join the Prophet's as a source.

lessons.title: Ijtihad and Taqlid
lessons.mainIdea: Ijtihad is a qualified scholar's independent reasoning; taqlid is following a school's settled view, and the balance between them is an old debate.
reading: *Ijtihad* means effort: a qualified jurist's independent reasoning from the sources to reach a ruling. *Taqlid* means following: accepting the settled view of one's school without redoing the reasoning. Classical scholars agreed that a mujtahid, a jurist able to perform ijtihad, needed deep knowledge of Arabic, the Qur'an, the hadith and the methods of law. An ordinary Muslim, they said, should practice taqlid, just as a patient follows a doctor.

A common story says that the 'gate of ijtihad' closed around the tenth century, after which Sunni scholars only followed their schools. Historians now doubt this. Wael Hallaq, in a much-cited 1984 article, argued that ijtihad never stopped; jurists kept issuing new rulings on new questions within their schools. What changed was that scholars stopped founding new schools and worked inside the four. The phrase 'closing of the gate' became popular among modern reformers who wanted to reopen it.

From the nineteenth century on, reformers such as Muhammad Abduh in Egypt argued that Muslims needed fresh ijtihad to meet railways, banks, printing and colonial rule. Some went further and rejected the schools altogether, calling for a return to the Qur'an and hadith alone; the Salafi movement drew on this call. Others defended the schools as a guard against amateurs reading the text however they liked. Both sides quoted the Qur'an and the Prophet's example.

Today the debate continues in every country with Muslims. Who is qualified to reason from the text? A trained scholar only, or any careful reader? Councils of scholars now issue collective rulings, a kind of shared ijtihad, on organ donation, in vitro fertilization and finance. Muslim writers disagree about whether that is the gate reopening or a new door.

words.d: a qualified jurist's independent reasoning from the sources to reach a ruling
following the settled view of a school of law without redoing the reasoning
a jurist qualified to perform ijtihad

look.title: Did the Gate Close?
look.text: Reading A: After about 950, Sunni jurists agreed that all the great questions had been settled and simply followed their schools; the gate of ijtihad closed. Reading B (Wael Hallaq, 1984): Jurists kept reasoning about new cases in every century; what ended was the founding of new schools, not independent reasoning itself.
look.prompt: What evidence would help you decide between these two readings of the history? Why might a modern reformer prefer to tell the story as Reading A?

check.why: Taqlid is following; ijtihad is a qualified jurist's own effort to reason from the sources.

check.why: Abduh and others argued the modern world needed new reasoning from the sources, not only inherited rulings.

sections.title: What the Law Covers, and Why

lessons.title: Family, Money and Contracts
lessons.mainIdea: Most of the Qur'an's legal verses concern worship, family and fair dealing, and jurists built detailed rules of marriage, inheritance and trade on them.
reading: The largest body of Qur'anic law after worship concerns the family. Surah 4, An-Nisa, 'Women,' and Surah 2 set rules for marriage, the bridal gift that a husband pays to his wife, divorce and the waiting period after it, and the support of children. Verse 4:11 lays out shares of *inheritance*: in general, a son receives twice a daughter's share, with fixed portions for parents and spouses. Muslim scholars note that this gave women a guaranteed share at a time when many Arabian women could inherit nothing. Modern Muslim readers debate whether the shares are fixed for all time or tied to an older economy in which men bore all the family's costs.

Money and trade receive careful attention. The longest verse in the Qur'an, 2:282, tells believers to write down a debt, name the due date and have witnesses. The Qur'an forbids *riba*, usually translated as usury or interest, in 2:275 and elsewhere. What counts as riba has been argued for centuries; modern Islamic finance builds contracts, such as shared-profit partnerships, that jurists accept as free of it. The Qur'an also demands honest weights and measures (83:1–3, Al-Mutaffifin) and the keeping of contracts (5:1, Al-Ma'idah).

From these verses jurists built the law of *contracts*: sale, lease, partnership, agency, pledge and gift, each with conditions. A sale required a clear price and a thing that existed and could be delivered; selling fish still in the sea was void because of uncertainty. Historians of law observe that Muslim merchants carried these rules along the trade routes to West Africa, India and Southeast Asia, and that many Muslim-majority countries still draw on them in their civil codes.

Family law is where the Qur'an's rules touch daily life most directly, and it is where modern reform has been most active. Since the twentieth century, countries from Tunisia to Indonesia have revised marriage and divorce law, some citing new ijtihad, others citing the objectives of the law that a later lesson explains. Muslim scholars stand on many sides of these reforms; describing that range is part of reading the verses accurately.

words.d: the division of a dead person's property; Qur'an 4:11 sets fixed shares for children, parents and spouses
usury or interest, forbidden by the Qur'an in 2:275; what exactly counts as riba is long debated
a binding agreement; Islamic law developed detailed rules for sale, lease, partnership and gift

look.title: Write Down the Debt
look.text: The Qur'an's longest verse tells believers that when they contract a debt for a fixed term, they should write it down; a scribe should record it fairly; the debtor should dictate it; and two witnesses should be called. If two men are not available, then one man and two women, so that if one forgets the other may remind her. It ends by saying that writing is fairer in God's sight and makes testimony surer.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:282, Al-Baqarah, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: What problems in a trading town might this verse be trying to prevent? Which parts of it have modern Muslim readers debated, and why?

Pay the bridal gift before marriage
Write down a debt, set its term and call witnesses
Divide an inheritance among sons only
check.why: The Qur'an's longest verse concerns recording debts in writing with witnesses.

check.q: What is riba?
choices: A contract of partnership
The waiting period after divorce
A fixed share of inheritance
Usury or interest, which the Qur'an forbids in 2:275
check.why: Riba is forbidden in 2:275; the exact scope of the term is debated, and Islamic finance designs contracts to avoid it.

check.q: Why would a classical jurist rule that selling fish still in the sea is void?
choices: The sale involves uncertainty, since the thing sold may not exist or be delivered

check.why: Contract law required a definite thing that could be delivered; excessive uncertainty voided a sale.

lessons.title: Crime and Punishment: The Hudud
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an fixes penalties for a handful of offenses, the hudud, and classical jurists surrounded them with strict conditions of proof.
reading: A small number of Qur'anic verses name a fixed punishment. Classical jurists called these the *hudud*, 'limits,' and counted them as offenses against God whose penalties a judge could not change. The Qur'an itself names theft (5:38, Al-Ma'idah: amputation of the hand), highway robbery (5:33), unlawful sexual intercourse (24:2, An-Nur: one hundred lashes), and falsely accusing someone of it (24:4: eighty lashes). Most schools added drinking wine, with a penalty drawn from hadith rather than the Qur'an. Stoning for adultery by a married person appears in hadith, not in the Qur'an's text; some modern Muslim scholars therefore reject it, and others defend it.

Classical jurists made these penalties very hard to apply. Unlawful intercourse required four eyewitnesses to the act itself; a confession could be withdrawn. Theft required that the goods be above a minimum value, taken from a secure place, and not taken in need; a well-known tradition says the caliph Umar suspended the penalty during a famine. Jurists quoted a hadith telling judges to avert the hudud wherever there was doubt. Historians who study court records from Ottoman and Mughal lands find the fixed penalties applied rarely.

Other crimes fell under *qisas*, retaliation, and *ta'zir*, discretionary punishment. For killing or wounding, 2:178 and 5:45 allow retaliation in kind but urge the victim's family to accept compensation or forgive, and 5:45 says forgiving is an atonement. Most crimes had no fixed penalty at all, and a judge set a punishment he thought fit, which could be a fine, prison or a reprimand.

In the modern world the hudud are among the most disputed parts of Islamic law. Most Muslim-majority countries do not apply them; a few do, and cases there draw wide attention. Some Muslim scholars argue that the conditions of proof cannot be met in a modern state and that the penalties should be suspended; others argue that they are God's fixed limits. Reading the verses in context means seeing both the text and the centuries of conditions built around it.

words.d: 'limits'; the few offenses for which the Qur'an fixes a penalty, such as theft and false accusation
retaliation in kind for killing or wounding, which the Qur'an allows while urging compensation or forgiveness
discretionary punishment set by a judge for offenses with no fixed penalty

look.title: Avert the Fixed Penalties in Doubt
look.text: A saying attributed to the Prophet, reported in the collection of al-Tirmidhi among others, tells judges to ward off the hudud from Muslims as much as they can, and adds that it is better for a ruler to err in pardoning than to err in punishing.
look.cite: Hadith reported by al-Tirmidhi (9th century), paraphrased; graded weak in its chain by some hadith scholars but widely cited by jurists
look.prompt: How might a rule like this shape the way a judge weighs the evidence in a theft case? Why might jurists have valued a report even when its chain of transmission was questioned?

check.q: Which of these penalties is found in the Qur'an's text itself?
choices: Stoning for adultery
Eighty lashes for falsely accusing someone of unlawful intercourse (24:4)
A penalty for drinking wine
Prison for tax evasion
check.why: 24:4 names eighty lashes; stoning and the wine penalty come from hadith, not from the Qur'an's text.

check.q: Why do historians say the hudud were rarely applied in classical courts?
choices: The Qur'an forbade judges from reading Surah 5
The penalties applied only to non-Muslims
Jurists set strict proof conditions, such as four eyewitnesses, and told judges to avert the penalties in doubt
Courts did not exist before 1800
check.why: Strict evidence rules and the principle of averting the hudud in doubt made the fixed penalties hard to impose.

check.q: What does the Qur'an urge in cases of killing, alongside allowing retaliation?
choices: That the killer be exiled to Mecca
That the judge apply four eyewitnesses
That the case be ignored
That the victim's family accept compensation or forgive
check.why: 2:178 and 5:45 permit qisas but encourage compensation and forgiveness, calling forgiveness an atonement.

lessons.title: The Purposes of the Law
lessons.mainIdea: The maqasid theory holds that the law exists to protect faith, life, mind, family and property, and modern reformers use it to argue for change.
reading: Why does the law say what it says? Some jurists asked this question directly and answered that God's law has purposes, *maqasid*. Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, who died in 1111, listed five things the law exists to protect: religion, life, intellect, lineage (family) and property. The prohibition of wine protects the mind; the rules of marriage protect the family; the penalty for theft protects property. Al-Ghazali argued that when a text was silent, a jurist could rule in favor of whatever protected these five.

The Andalusian scholar Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi, who died in 1388 in Granada, made the maqasid the center of a whole theory of law. He sorted human needs into three levels: necessities, needs and improvements. He argued that jurists should read the Qur'an's rules in the light of what they are for, not only in the light of their words. For centuries his work was little read; in the twentieth century it became one of the most cited books in Islamic legal reform.

Modern reformers use the maqasid to argue that a ruling made for one time can be changed to serve the same purpose in another. If the inheritance shares were meant to secure fairness in a world where men paid all the family's costs, some argue, then fairness now may require different shares. Their critics reply that purposes are easy to invent and that a jurist who reads for purpose may end up overriding the text. Both camps say they are being faithful to the Qur'an.

The maqasid debate is one of the main live questions in Islamic law today, from Cairo's Al-Azhar university to think tanks in London and Virginia. Reading about it, students can watch a tradition argue with itself about how to read its own book, which is what the study of a sacred text in history mostly looks like.

words.d: the purposes or objectives of the law; classically, protecting religion, life, intellect, family and property
scholar who died in 1111 and listed the five things the law protects
Andalusian scholar (d. 1388) who built a theory of law around the maqasid, much cited by modern reformers

look.title: Milestones of Legal Theory
look.cite: Death dates of the authors, as given in standard histories of Islamic law
look.prompt: The maqasid idea was stated in 1111 but became central only in the twentieth century. What might make an old idea suddenly useful?

check.q: Which five things did al-Ghazali say the law exists to protect?
choices: Religion, life, intellect, lineage and property
Land, water, trade, poetry and tribe
The caliph, the army, the treasury, the mosque and the market
Prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, alms and testimony
check.why: Al-Ghazali's five purposes, the maqasid, are religion, life, intellect, lineage (family) and property.

check.q: How do modern reformers use the maqasid?
choices: To prove that the four schools were never valid
To argue that a ruling can change if the change serves the same purpose in a new setting
To count the verses of the Qur'an
To settle the order of the surahs
check.why: Reformers read rules by their purpose and argue that serving the purpose may require a different rule today.

check.q: What is the main objection critics raise against reading the law by its purposes?
choices: Al-Shatibi was not a Muslim
Purposes exist only in Shia law
Purposes can be invented, and a jurist may end up overriding the text
The Qur'an forbids asking why
check.why: Critics warn that reasoning from purpose can become a way to set aside what the text plainly says.

lessons.title: Sharia in the Headlines and in America
lessons.mainIdea: The word sharia means different things to scholars, states and headlines, and Muslim jurists in the United States apply the tradition mostly to personal and community life.
reading: The word sharia now appears in news stories, laws and campaign speeches, often as a single thing. For Muslim scholars it is not one thing. It is God's way as they understand it, worked out through fiqh that differs by school, place and century. When a Muslim in Chicago says she follows sharia, she usually means that she prays, fasts, avoids interest on loans where she can, and marries and gives to charity by its rules. When a headline says a country 'imposes sharia,' it usually means one government's chosen set of fiqh rules, often the criminal ones.

In the United States, Islamic law has no force as state law. Courts apply American law. Muslim jurists here work in other ways. Since the late twentieth century, bodies such as the Fiqh Council of North America have issued opinions on questions Muslims in America ask: when Ramadan begins, whether a mortgage is allowed, how to handle organ donation. A *fatwa*, a scholar's opinion, binds no one; it is advice a Muslim may follow or seek elsewhere. Mosques and Islamic centers in the Chicago area, one of the country's larger Muslim communities, host scholars who answer such questions.

Some Muslim couples ask an imam or a scholar to mediate a dispute, or write an Islamic marriage contract alongside the civil one. American courts sometimes enforce such contracts as ordinary agreements, the way they enforce other religious contracts. Between 2010 and 2020, several states passed laws banning courts from considering 'foreign law' or sharia; legal scholars across the spectrum have noted that these laws mostly address a situation that does not arise, since courts already apply the Constitution first.

For a student of the Qur'an, the point is that the same word carries different weights in different mouths. A jurist means a method and a body of reasoning. A government means the rules it has chosen to enforce. A headline may mean a fear. Reading well means asking, each time, which sharia is being discussed and whose reading of the Qur'an stands behind it.

words.d: a scholar's legal opinion, given in answer to a question; it advises but does not bind
a body of Muslim scholars that issues opinions on questions Muslims in the United States and Canada ask
in Sunni usage, a prayer leader or mosque scholar; in Shia usage, one of the divinely guided successors of the Prophet

look.title: Three People Say 'Sharia'
look.text: A Chicago nurse says, 'I try to live by sharia,' meaning her prayers, her fasting and how she handles money. A government spokesman says, 'We have implemented sharia,' meaning a criminal code his ministry drafted. A newspaper headline reads, 'Sharia comes to town,' beside a photo of a new mosque. All three use one word.
look.prompt: What does each speaker mean? What would you ask each one to find out whose reading of the Qur'an stands behind their use of the word?

check.q: What is a fatwa?
choices: A law passed by a Muslim-majority country
A fixed Qur'anic penalty
A verse abrogated by a later one
A scholar's opinion on a legal question, which advises but does not bind
check.why: A fatwa is advisory; a Muslim may follow it or seek another scholar's view.

check.q: What role does Islamic law have in United States courts?
choices: None as state law; courts apply American law, though they may enforce a religious contract as an ordinary agreement
It replaces state law in family cases
It applies only in Chicago
Judges must consult the Fiqh Council
check.why: American courts apply the Constitution and state law; an Islamic marriage contract may be enforced only as a contract.

check.q: Why do many Muslim scholars object to headlines that treat sharia as a single thing?
choices: Because sharia is a secret teaching
Because sharia is worked out through fiqh that differs by school, place and century
Because the word does not appear in Arabic
Because only Shia Muslims use the term
check.why: Scholars distinguish God's way from the many human readings of it, and note that a headline usually means one government's chosen rules.

review.q: About how many of the Qur'an's roughly 6,236 verses do scholars count as legal?
choices: About 3,000
Nearly all of them
A few hundred, with estimates from about 200 to 500
Fewer than ten
review.why: Estimates vary, but legal verses are a small share of the whole, concentrated in the Medina surahs.

review.q: In the Sunni ranking of sources, which comes immediately after the Qur'an?
choices: Analogy
Consensus
The rulings of the Imams
The Sunnah, known through hadith
review.why: Al-Shafi'i's order is Qur'an, Sunnah, ijma', qiyas.

review.q: Which school is named for a scholar who died in 855 and preferred hadith to reasoned opinion?
choices: Hanbali
Hanafi
Maliki
Ja'fari
review.why: Ahmad ibn Hanbal (d. 855) gave hadith priority; the Hanbali school follows him.

review.q: What source does the Ja'fari school use in place of Sunni analogy?
choices: Custom of the Meccan tribes
Reason (aql) and the teachings of the Imams
Roman law
The consensus of the Ottoman court
review.why: Shia jurists mostly rejected qiyas and relied on aql and the Imams' reports.

review.q: The theory of naskh, or abrogation, explains which sequence of verses?
choices: The verses on inheritance in 4:11
The Throne Verse and the Fatiha
The verses on wine, ending in the command to shun it (5:90)
The verses on debts in 2:282
review.why: Classical jurists read 2:219, 4:43 and 5:90 as a sequence ending in prohibition.

review.q: Which of these is required in classical fiqh to prove unlawful intercourse?
choices: One witness and a written note
A judge's suspicion
A confession from a relative
Four eyewitnesses to the act itself
review.why: The strict four-witness rule is one reason the fixed penalties were rarely applied.

review.q: Al-Shatibi (d. 1388) is best known for which idea?
choices: Reading the law by its purposes, the maqasid
Closing the gate of ijtihad
Founding the Maliki school
Collecting the Shia hadith
review.why: Al-Shatibi built a theory of law around the objectives it serves; modern reformers cite him often.

review.q: What is the difference between a fatwa and a law in a Muslim-majority country?
choices: A fatwa is enforced and a law is optional
A fatwa is a scholar's advisory opinion; a state law is enforced by the government
They are the same thing
A fatwa comes only from the caliph
review.why: Fatwas advise and do not bind; states choose which fiqh rules to enforce as law.
